summary: A second submission from Robert C. Millington, 52 pages dated 3 August, published here in full and widening his first analysis from maritime law to all four transport modes. Two things in it matter more than the rest, because they cut against what this archive published from his first document. He now sets out a manifest duty that does exist — Cap. 49:03 s. 7(1), requiring the master to declare in writing the number, names, sex and age of every person on board before clearance, with a year's imprisonment for a false declaration — where this site had published his earlier finding that no counting duty exists in Guyanese law. And he places the vessel inside Part X of the Shipping Act, on the ground that a mechanically propelled steel passenger ferry is none of the six exceptions in s. 297, where his first analysis turned on a 24-metre band this document does not mention. He describes neither as a correction and does not refer to the earlier submission at all. Beyond that: an annual survey duty in terms, a Certificate of Seaworthiness regime from which State vessels are exempted by five words he says could be deleted by regulation tomorrow, a second route into survey through the Tax Act licence that does reach State vessels, ten inconsistent capacity rules, a schedule of 52 deficiencies across the four modes, and a warning that the 2022 Revised Edition of the Laws was laid before the National Assembly twenty-nine days before the ship went down.

The terms of reference have been published in the Extraordinary Gazette, closing the gap this site has recorded since 26 July. Six heads — seaworthiness, passenger and cargo operations, crew qualifications and conduct, search and rescue effectiveness, regulatory oversight by state entities, and human factors — with a two-month deadline for final written findings, public hearings, a power to issue interim safety reports, and explicit authority to refer evidence of criminal negligence, official misconduct or statutory breaches straight to prosecuting authorities. The inclusion of regulatory oversight answers part of Christopher Ram's objection that the inquiry stopped at the voyage. Still absent: a Statutory Instrument number, a budget, and any resolution of whether the terms reach loading authorisation and procurement as well as execution. And the deadline now sits awkwardly against the salvage timetable, since a lift is not expected to begin before late August.

A secretary has been named — attorney Javed Shadick — closing a gap Demerara Waves recorded as open on 30 July, and the appointment drew an immediate independence objection from David Patterson. The reported ties are three: he is the son of a former PPP minister and GECOM Commissioner, he is currently Secretary of the Constitution Reform Commission, and he holds a function in the Guyana Civil Aviation Authority. The third is the one that matters most here, because the Civil Aviation Authority sits under the Ministry of Public Utilities and Aviation — the ministry MARAD answers to, and MARAD's regulatory oversight is one of the six heads the Commission has just been empowered to investigate. Patterson also makes a timing point that is checkable against the record: the commissioners accept the wreck must be raised and examined, and have given themselves two months. No government response appears, and this is the second set of conflict questions about this Commission to go unanswered in five days.
